related_sources.source_text: Kimi K3.1 Pro vs Opus 5.5! https://t.co/nIrYcuEVvS

Kimi K3.1 Pro is the best open model in the world right now. No contest. But it's practically unusable on its own subscription.

I was on the $39 plan. I built the ship test, easily the best result I've seen from an open model, but it ate 11.6% of my monthly quota. That means I can build something like this about 8 times a month, with zero fixes. That's insane.

On most $20 plans the same job doesn't even hit 10% of the weekly limit, and with some, like Claude, it doesn't even hit 10% of the 5-hour limit. Worst subscription out there, hands down. I regret the $39 and I know I'll get nothing out of it.

The bottleneck isn't quality. It's compute.

What it does well:
It thinks through every possibility better than any model I've used. It beats DeepSeek V4 Pro, trades blows with Qwen3.8-Max and even pulls ahead in some areas, and it's miles ahead of GLM-5.3. Not even the same league. Computer use got a big upgrade too. It might be the best open model at it, alongside MiniMax.

Where it falls short:
It doesn't know when to go long and when to keep it short. It skimps when you need detail, then dumps bullet points on you like a model from two or three years ago. And it's slow. Painfully slow. We're talking 3-4x slower, which makes it rough as an executor. I'd use it to write or review a plan, then hand execution to another model.

How I'll actually use it:
Outside Kimi, 100%. Mostly in Devin, maybe Droid too. Droid served a heavily quantized Kimi K3 last time and performance tanked, so I'm hoping Factory ships a better version this round. For now, Kimi in Devin looks like the sweet spot for price and quality.

Over Astra? Every day. It's roughly 5x cheaper, so on Devin or API credits it's a no-brainer. Over Claude Opus 5.5? In a neutral harness or a subscription that offers both, there's real value at about half the price. But Kimi's subscription vs Claude's? There's no reason to pick Kimi.

I can't recommend the direct subscription. Period.

cases.title: Layered holographic card shader
cases.takeaway: Build and validate one shader layer at a time.
cases.body_notes: The author describes a Three.js plane, view-dependent diffraction, independently tested foil patterns, adjustable controls, canvas export and a self-review fix. cases.source_text:
I turned a Pokémon card from my binder into a real holographic shader with Kimi K3.1 Pro and Three.js. 

Diffraction grating, 8 foil patterns, drag to tilt. $2.10 and 38 minutes.

The rule that made it work: never ask for "A holo card shader". Ask for one layer at a time.

Step 1 -> One card texture from my own binder, a plane in Three.js, orbit controls. Nothing shiny yet.

Step 2 -> The diffraction grating itself in a single prompt: a rainbow that moves with the view angle, not a static gradient.

Step 3 -> Foil patterns as toggles: hairline, pillar beams, crosshatch, cracked ice, glitter, water ripple, cat eye. One prompt each, test each one before the next.

Step 4 -> Sliders for foil exposure, star intensity, pattern scale. Auto-rotate on a Lissajous path so it never sits still.

Step 5 -> Export PNG and WebM straight from the canvas, so the card can leave the browser.

Step 6 -> K3.1 Pro reviews its own shader, finds the banding on the cat-eye pattern, fixes it before I even notice.

The split:

> Three.js: the plane, the camera, the controls.
> GLSL: every pattern, written by K3.1 Pro.
> K3.1 Pro: the shader math, the UI, the fixes.
> Me: tilt the card and decide which foil looks real.

The part that matters: the whole thing cost about half of what Opus 5.5 charges for the same session and roughly 5x less than GPT-6 Astra, and on the high-speed version the shader came back in seconds, not minutes.

Commit after every pattern that works. A bad prompt costs seconds, not an evening.

@Kimi_Moonshot's new reasoning model gains 11 points over Kimi K3 (max, 44). It trails only Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback, 58), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback, 56), and Muse Wonder Full (max, 56) on the Intelligence Index.

Once the weights for K3.1 Pro are released it will be the highest-scoring open weights model and the gap between the leading open weights and proprietary models on the Intelligence Index will narrow from 12 points to 3.

Key results:
➤ Large gains in agentic performance: Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 3rd on GDPval-AA with 1,846 Elo, up 312 Elo from Kimi K3, behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (1,866 Elo) and Muse Wonder Full (1,857 Elo). Kimi K3.1 Pro also achieves the highest score of any model on Terminal-Bench 4.0. K3.1 Pro scores 67%, up from 13% for Kimi K3 and ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (64%). AutomationBench-AA, which tests agentic SaaS workflows, rises from 58% to 73%.

➤ Gains in other evals are more moderate: Humanity's Last Exam rises from 47% to 52%, CritPt from 23% to 25%, and SciCode from 59% to 61%. AA-Omniscience Index rises from 20 to 30, as the hallucination rate falls from 53% to 44% and accuracy rises from 48% to 51%.

➤ Cost per Task roughly equal to Kimi K3 at $1.98 per Task: K3.1 Pro uses 55K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, 14% more than Kimi K3 at 48K, while its first-party token prices are 33% lower.

Additional model details:
➤ Context window: 1M tokens.
➤ Size: 2.8T total, 104B active parameters
➤ Input modalities: Text and image
➤ Weights and license: Weights currently not published, Moonshot is expected to release the weights soon after launch
➤ Pricing: $2/$10/$0.20 per 1M input/output/cache hit tokens, 33% lower than Kimi K3 on all three rates.

Congratulations to the team at @Kimi_Moonshot on the release!
